summary:
Five evals were run (45 iterations total, no failures). One eval ("unrelated-question-negative") was a should_trigger:false test and was fully skipped for expected_output/assertions/metrics/comparison — it only confirms both variants correctly avoided firing, so it contributes no differentiating data.

Across the remaining four evals, a consistent and notable pattern emerges: without_skill shows 0/5 expected-output pass rate in three of the four evals (troubleshoot-no-audit-logs-in-s3, interpret-compliance-report, reason-about-anomaly-alert) and 1/5 in the fourth (troubleshoot-reports-not-generated), compared to with_skill's 3/5 (60%) in all four. This is a fairly consistent gap, though the underlying confidence on these expected-output judgments is only medium-to-high, not uniformly high, so some caution is warranted. Notably, in three of these four evals, without_skill has no assertion-level data at all (marked null) — meaning per-assertion pass/fail comparisons could not be computed for without_skill in those cases, so the size of the quality gap is only partially visible through assertions; it is visible mainly through the aggregate expected_output pass rate.

Where assertion-level data does exist for both variants (troubleshoot-reports-not-generated and reason-about-anomaly-alert), with_skill passed more assertions overall (10/12 and 14/16) than without_skill (2/4 and 2/8). Some individual assertions passed for both variants equally (e.g., checking the Lambda's schedule/timeout, checking logs for errors, and explaining that audit logs in S3 can be investigated further — these "always_passes" items don't differentiate the variants). Others were "flaky" (inconsistent pass/fail across runs for one or both variants, e.g., referencing the monthly-reports S3 prefix, or stating there's no persisted anomaly-findings file), and one assertion in reason-about-anomaly-alert showed a clean split: with_skill passed all 4 relevant runs on referencing anomaly detection categories/thresholds while without_skill passed 0/2 — a case where the two variants diverge in a way not overshadowed by other differences. In troubleshoot-no-audit-logs-in-s3, one assertion (inspecting the log-processor Lambda's logs for errors) failed for with_skill on all 4 evaluated runs, and no comparable without_skill data exists — an assertion neither variant clearly satisfies (or at least not confirmed for without_skill), suggesting that specific behavior may need work regardless of variant.

Quality-comparison pairs (head-to-head judged comparisons) were mostly skipped: 0 of 5 pairs evaluated in three evals, and only 1 of 5 evaluated in troubleshoot-reports-not-generated, where that single pair favored without_skill on accuracy, actionability, and completeness (high confidence). This is a very thin sample (n=1) and shouldn't be read as a general quality verdict.

On runtime and cost, results are mixed and modest in size: with_skill was slower/costlier in troubleshoot-no-audit-logs-in-s3 (68s/$0.57 vs without_skill's 0s/$0.00 — but without_skill's 0s/$0.00 likely reflects it not producing a comparable run rather than a real speed advantage, given its 0/5 expected-output rate) and interpret-compliance-report (13s/$0.11 vs 0s/$0.00, same caveat), while in troubleshoot-reports-not-generated with_skill was slightly slower (31s vs 25s, $0.26 vs $0.21) and in reason-about-anomaly-alert with_skill was actually faster (34s vs 42s, $0.28 vs $0.35). Context window utilization was similar and low for both variants throughout (roughly 3.6%-4.3%), with no compaction events.

Output consistency (run-to-run stability) was only measurable for with_skill in two evals (troubleshoot-no-audit-logs-in-s3 and interpret-compliance-report), both rated "mostly_consistent" with high confidence; no consistency data was available for without_skill in any eval, and none for with_skill in the other two evals, so consistency comparisons are largely incomplete.

Overall, the clearest and most repeated signal is that without_skill's expected-output pass rate was low (0-20%) versus with_skill's more moderate 60% across the four applicable evals, and where assertion data exists, with_skill passed more assertions. However, several caveats limit how strongly this should be weighed: assertion-level data for without_skill is missing in most evals, the one available head-to-head quality comparison (n=1) favored without_skill, and runtime/cost differences are small and partly confounded by missing runs for without_skill. Some assertions pass for both or fail for both regardless of variant, indicating those specific test criteria aren't distinguishing the two systems well or represent shared weaknesses to address."

troubleshoot-no-audit-logs-in-s3.summary:
This eval covered a single chat task, with the triggering behavior firing in all 5 runs for both variants (trigger_fired: 5/5) — so the scenario itself was reliably exercised.

Beyond that, the two variants diverge sharply, but with important caveats about data completeness:

- Expected output: with_skill met the expected output in 3/5 runs (60%, medium confidence). without_skill met it in 0/5 runs (0%). This is a notable gap, but it rests on only 5 runs per variant, and with_skill's own confidence in the judgment is only "medium," not high, so some caution is warranted even on this seemingly clear result.

- Assertions: Only with_skill has per-assertion data (13/20 pass, 65% overall); without_skill has no assertion data at all (null), meaning we cannot compare pass rates side by side. Looking at with_skill's individual assertions, results are mixed and reveal specific weaknesses rather than a uniform picture: it fully passed checks on CloudWatch Logs export detection (4/4) and following a logical pipeline order (4/4), reasonably passed the pgAudit/database-auditing check (3/4), but failed entirely on inspecting the log-processor Lambda's logs for errors (0/4), and only half-passed naming the log-processor Lambda correctly (2/4). This shows that even with_skill's moderate 60% expected-output rate is driven by clear, specific gaps rather than random noise. All these per-assertion patterns are marked "inconclusive," and since without_skill has no corresponding data, none of these assertions actually differentiate the two variants — they only characterize with_skill.

- Quality comparison: No quality pairs could be evaluated (0 evaluated, 5 skipped), so there is no head-to-head quality signal available at all for this eval.

- Metrics: with_skill averaged 1m8s runtime and $0.57 cost per run; without_skill shows 0s runtime and $0.00 cost. This near-zero metric for without_skill, combined with its 0/5 expected-output pass rate and null assertions, suggests without_skill may not have produced substantive output in these runs (e.g., not engaging with the task) rather than simply being "faster/cheaper" — this should be treated as missing/degenerate data rather than an efficiency advantage. Context window utilization was low and similar for both (4.3% vs 3.7%), with no compaction events for either.

- Consistency: with_skill was rated "mostly_consistent" across runs (score 2.0, high confidence in that judgment). without_skill has no consistency data (null).

Overall, this is a case where most of the comparative machinery (assertions, quality pairs, consistency) only produced usable data for with_skill, while without_skill registered a trigger fire but otherwise shows empty or zero-value results across expected-output, assertions, metrics, and consistency. This pattern points to a data or execution gap for without_skill in this eval rather than a meaningful performance comparison, so no reliable side-by-side judgment on quality or capability can be drawn here — only that with_skill produced measurable, partially-passing output while without_skill's outputs were not captured or did not meet the expected-output bar in any run.

answer_consistency.reasoning: All five outputs agree on the core root cause: the Aurora cluster is stopped, which halts log generation and thus the CloudWatch->Lambda->S3 pipeline. All mention the stopped cluster ID, the auto-restart around 2026-09-28, and reference an S3/permissions gap in verifying. This is a material factual divergence, not just omission style, so it goes beyond mostly_consistent into more divergence, but since the primary answer (stopped cluster) is consistent across all, and only 2 of 5 diverge on the secondary root cause, I'll rate mostly_consistent leaning toward inconsistent boundary — given the contradiction is material (pgAudit fine vs pgAudit broken), this pushes toward inconsistent for iterations 2 and 5 vs 1 and 4.

Iteration 5 recommends confirming intent (planned vs unexpected stop) which isn't emphasized elsewhere. All offer some form of follow-up investigation into why the cluster stopped, but the specifics differ across outputs.

Otherwise the shape (headers, bullets, next steps list, closing question) is broadly the same across all five.

troubleshoot-reports-not-generated.summary:
Overview: This eval ran a chat task 5 times per variant, checking a scenario about diagnosing a report-generator Lambda (schedule/timeout, logs, and the S3 monthly-reports location).

Trigger: The behavior under test fired in 4/5 runs overall (80%) — this metric wasn't split by variant, so it's a shared baseline condition rather than a per-variant result.

Expected output: with_skill met the expected output in 3/5 runs (60%, high confidence in that judgment), while without_skill met it in 1/5 runs (20%, medium confidence). This is a notable gap in favor of with_skill, though the medium confidence on without_skill's judgment means that result is somewhat less certain than with_skill's.

Assertions: with_skill passed 10/12 assertion checks (83%) vs without_skill's 2/4 (50%) — note the very different denominators (12 vs 4 checks total), reflecting that without_skill had fewer eligible runs/assertions to evaluate, so these rates aren't fully apples-to-apples. Looking at the individual assertions:
- Two assertions ("checks schedule/timeout" and "checks logs for errors") passed 100% of the time for both variants — these aren't differentiating the variants, both handle these consistently well.
- Two assertions ("references reports bucket and monthly-reports prefix" and "references the monthly-reports S3 prefix") were flaky for with_skill (67% pass) and failed outright for without_skill (0%, though only 1 run was evaluated). This is the main area of divergence and where without_skill struggled.

Quality comparison: Only 1 of 5 pairs could be evaluated for head-to-head quality (4 were skipped, likely due to missing outputs or non-matching runs), so this comparison rests on a very small sample. In that single evaluated pair, without_skill was favored across all three criteria (accuracy, actionability, completeness) with high confidence. Given the tiny sample size (n=1), this should be treated as a single data point, not a robust trend — it also runs counter to the expected-output and assertion results, which favored with_skill overall.

Runtime and cost: without_skill was faster (~25s vs ~31s, about 6s difference) and cheaper (~$0.21 vs ~$0.26). Neither exceeded the 30s runtime threshold in the one evaluated pair. Context window utilization was low and similar for both (~3.7% vs ~4.0%), with no compaction events for either.

Output consistency: Not available for either variant (both null), so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed from this data.

Overall picture: The dimensions point in different directions. with_skill more consistently met the expected output and passed the differentiating assertions (particularly around referencing the correct S3 prefix), while without_skill was faster and cheaper, and won the single small-sample quality comparison. Two assertions showed no difference (both variants always pass), one behavior (S3 prefix referencing) was clearly weaker for without_skill, and the quality-comparison and expected-output findings are based on small samples (1 pair; 5 runs) with mixed confidence levels, so these results should be viewed as suggestive rather than conclusive.

Key observations:

- Expected output: with_skill met the expected output in 3/5 runs (60%), with high-confidence judgments and no low-confidence flags — a reasonably solid measurement showing partial but incomplete success. without_skill met the expected output in 0/5 runs (0%). However, without_skill has no assertion data, no metrics of substance (0s runtime, $0.00 cost), and no consistency score — strongly suggesting without_skill's run did not actually produce a comparable output (e.g., the trigger or task path didn't execute for it), rather than reflecting a genuine substantive failure. This 0/5 should be read with caution as a sign of missing/absent data, not a confirmed quality shortfall.

- Assertions: All 12 sub-assertions passed for with_skill (100%), spanning both LLM-judged criteria (report sections described, S3 location referenced, findings tied to anomaly categories/severities) and a regex check for the S3 bucket path. All were rated high confidence where applicable. No assertion data exists for without_skill at all, so no side-by-side pass/fail comparison could be made on any individual criterion — this is an absence of data, not a without_skill failure on those specific checks.

- Quality comparison: 0 of 5 pairs were evaluated for relative quality; all 5 were skipped. No head-to-head quality signal is available.

- Metrics: with_skill averaged 13s runtime and $0.11 cost with 4.0% context utilization; without_skill showed 0s and $0.00 cost with 3.6% utilization. The near-zero runtime/cost for without_skill reinforces that it likely did not execute meaningful work in this eval, rather than being a more "efficient" run.

- Consistency: with_skill's outputs were "mostly consistent" across runs (score 2.33/3, with 1 dimension fully consistent and 2 mostly consistent), rated with high confidence. No consistency data exists for without_skill.

Overall state: This is not a balanced A/B comparison — nearly all substantive data (assertions, quality pairs, consistency, and most metrics) exists only for with_skill, which performed solidly on the fully-specified checks (100% assertion pass rate, mostly consistent output) but only partially met the overall expected-output bar (60%). without_skill's complete absence of assertion/quality/consistency data and near-zero runtime/cost strongly suggest the eval did not fully execute for without_skill, making its 0% expected-output figure unreliable as a performance signal. No dimension here supports a comparative judgment between the two variants; the main finding is a data gap for without_skill.

reason-about-anomaly-alert.summary:
This eval covered a single chat task about explaining anomaly-detection/audit records (SNS alerts, monthly reports, S3 audit logs), run 5 times per variant.

Trigger: The behavior under test fired in 4/5 runs overall (this metric isn't broken out by variant).

Expected output: There is a large, high-confidence difference here. with_skill met the expected output in 3/5 runs (60%), while without_skill met it in 0/5 runs (0%). Confidence in these judgments is high for both, so this gap looks like a genuine measured difference rather than noise in the judging itself, though the underlying sample size is small (5 runs each).

Per-assertion results reinforce this but also reveal nuance:
- One assertion ("audit logs in S3 can be read to investigate further") passed for both variants at or near 100% — this assertion is not distinguishing the variants.
- Two assertions (about the "no separate persisted anomaly-findings file" point, and about SNS alert/monthly report being the durable records) show a "flaky" pattern: with_skill passed 3/4 instances and without_skill passed 0/2. Both are imperfect, but without_skill failed these consistently in the runs measured while with_skill mostly passed.
- One assertion (referencing anomaly detection categories/thresholds) is a clean split: with_skill passed 4/4, without_skill passed 0/2 — a case where one variant fully satisfies a criterion and the other fully fails it.
- Overall assertion pass rate: with_skill 14/16 (88%), without_skill 2/8 (25%), with all reported confidences high or medium (no low-confidence flags noted).

Metrics: with_skill ran faster (~34s vs ~42s, an ~8s difference) and cheaper (~$0.28 vs ~$0.35) on average. Context window utilization was nearly identical (~4% for both, no compaction for either). These are modest metric differences and, combined with with_skill's higher expected-output and assertion pass rates, do not represent a case of one variant trading speed for quality in the opposite direction — here with_skill was both faster/cheaper and scored higher on correctness in this run.

Quality comparison and consistency: No head-to-head quality comparison data is available — all 5 pairs were skipped, so there's no direct quality-favored signal one way or the other. Output consistency across repeated runs is also not available (null) for both variants, so we cannot say how stable each variant's phrasing/content was run-to-run beyond what the pass-rate variance implies.

Overall, the measured signal in this single eval favors with_skill on expected-output match and assertion pass rate, with matching or favorable metrics (runtime, cost) as well. However, sample sizes are small (5 runs, 2-4 assertion instances per item), quality-comparison and consistency data are entirely missing, and one assertion showed no differentiation at all — so this should be read as a directional finding from a limited dataset rather than a robust, multi-dimensional verdict.
